title: 7 Factors 4 Energy Cont
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The teacher invites the group to reflect on what supports or hinders their intention to sit daily, using energy as a starting point for this inquiry. They encourage mindfulness and self-awareness, drawing from the Buddha's teachings that cultivating energy requires acknowledging the states of misery caused by laziness and surrounding oneself with positive influences. The practice involves deliberately cultivating inner energy through noble examples, appreciating support, and inclining one's mind towards mindfulness. This approach aims to help individuals overcome obstacles and find serenity in their daily sitting practice.

It was fun.
And I was just really appreciating the unlikeliness of all this.
I was really appreciating how unlikely it is that all this could be happening.
It's sort of amazing.
And this is happening in all different ways, not just in this particular context.
A few hours ago, was it just a few hours ago?

Not to take for granted that you don't have wonderful new things to learn from sitting down for ten minutes.

And she was in her late 80s.
Yeah.
So we're really lucky.
Most of us are not yet in our late 80s.
So we're getting there.
Some of us are getting there.

So strange.
Miracle as always.
The dharma.

Tonight we'll linger a little longer on energy.
The third item, the third mental factor, the third quality of normal human beings that we all have.
We all have these qualities.
It's not something new we're trying to invent or create out of whole cloth.
It's something that we're inquiring into and curious about, seeing if we can nurture and support and uncover it.
So, energy.

We're thinking about what facilitates our energy coming forth and our engagement with the things that we know benefit us, and what obscures and hinders the coming forth of energy.
We were talking a little bit about energy and effort as the two halves of a similar process.
Effort seems a little more deliberate and directed by the self, and energy seems a little more mysterious, arising according to conditions.
It doesn't seem like we can really make energy exactly, but it does seem like we can influence the conditions, so that it's more likely that energy will arise in our life.

Some things take more gas than others.

Can I do this?

Hopefully we sleep at night, if we're lucky.
And then we get a new tank of gas.

It's not always that way.

It would be good for you, and all those tapes are playing.
Sometimes you sag and you're down for the count.
But other times somehow you rally and you do go out and exercise.
And after you exercise, almost always, we were agreeing, you seem to have more energy.
So how could that be?
You push harder on the gas, you get yourself over a little speed bump or something, and instead of the gas tank being used up, the gas tank is magically refilled.
So it seemed worthwhile to daylight our attitudes about energy and our frames around energy and see if they're actually true.
Maybe we just have some ways of thinking about our energy that are metaphors.
We think metaphorically, right?
They may or may not be helpful.
So we reflected on that, and my suggestion was that we look at our healthy intentions and look at what seems to allow them to occur or not.
The one possible specific intention we thought we might look at together is daily sitting.
We were also reflecting on the five hindrances as a way to understand what hinders us, since the hindrances, well, they hinder, right?
We have a list of five.
I've re-translated them a little bit into two pairs and one at the end.
The two pairs are desire and aversion; the second pair is dullness and restlessness.

Some of us might have taken that on, or some of us might not have been here.

What seemed to support that possibility?
What seemed to hinder that possibility?
And if you don't, in fact, hold that intention to sit every day, you might substitute some other healthy thing that you intend to do daily or regularly.
So let's cast our minds back.
What happened this morning?
What happened last night?
What happened yesterday?
As best we can remember, think about that for a moment.

Get really close to each other.

And let's have a little conversation.

A list of reflections, and I can print this out for you later.
I didn't manage it.

Start with that.
Really feel into that.
But then, as an antidote to that, we can reflect on the benefits of energy, the benefits of bringing up our energy.
There are ten items.
The second one is to reflect on the benefits of energy.
The third one is to remember the noble ones.
That's the way it's translated.
Remember those that are great examples and exemplars of practice.
And then in addition to remembering the noble ones, the fourth is to remember the noble heritage.
Remember the lineage.
Remember what we have received, and appreciate and reflect on that.
We're not so good at these kinds of reflections.
See, there are things to reflect on.
We receive this lineage.
Amazing.
The fifth is to reflect on and appreciate all the support that we have.
The support that we already have.
We tend to think about what more support we want.
But this is to reflect on the support we already have: the many people and circumstances and many areas where we have good fortune that support our life.

Avoid people who are drinking.
Similar idea, I guess.
Avoid people who are...
Maybe there are ways you can be with them to help them.

Spend time with energetic friends, the Buddha suggested.

Inclining the mind towards the development of energy.

What are the inner causes and conditions?
And how are you working with the mind?
So those are ten ways to work with your energy.

The practice of mindfulness provides us with information.

Four items.

The second is to avoid unmindful people.
The third is to choose mindful friends.

Not just leave that to chance.
So that's interesting.

I don't think he means that.

Polish.

Scowling, grimacing, waking up at night, muttering at dawn.
What oppressed me so much was a bit shameful.
Talking of it aloud would show neither tact nor prudence.
It might even seem an outrage against the health of mankind.
Alas, my memory does not want to leave me.
And in it, live beings, each with its own pain, each with its own dying, its own trepidation.
Why then innocence on paradisal beaches,*
*an impeccable sky over the church of hygiene?
Is it because that was long ago?
To a saintly man, so goes an Arab tale, God said, somewhat maliciously, had I revealed to people how great a sinner you are, they could not praise you.
And I, answered the pious one, had I unveiled to them how merciful you are, they would not care for you.
